FortiGate Log Analyzer - Manual

A single-file, no-install Windows tool for triaging FortiGate / FortiOS logs exactly as they come off the appliance. Point it at a folder of exported logs and it answers the questions an incident responder asks of a firewall: who logged in to it, what changed, who came in over VPN, what was exposed, what left, and what the security profiles caught.

Author: Ben Morris github.com/bpmorris22/FortiGate-Log-Analyzer MIT licence App v0.3.0 Manual updated 2026-10-18 All screenshots use synthetic data (firewall FGT-ACME-01, documentation IP ranges)

1  What it answers

Who logged in to the firewall? - every admin login attempt per source and username, each successful session, and whether the management interface is reachable from the Internet.
What changed? - every configuration change: path, object, old → new attributes, who made it and from where.
Who came in over VPN? - SSL-VPN logins per user and source country, password guessing, and IPsec peers (including Internet IKE scanning).
What was exposed, and what left? - inbound sessions the firewall accepted, internal admin-port fan-out (lateral movement), the largest uploads, Internet destinations by bytes out.
What did the security profiles catch - and what did they let through? - antivirus, IPS, application control, web filter and SSL inspection, with every event's outcome mapped to blocked / allowed / unknown.
Log folderGUI downloads / syslog / FAZ raw

It is part of the DFIR toolkit family (DFIR Windows Artifact Finder, the EZ-tool wrappers, Hayabusa, Hawk, UAC, vSphere and Data Domain triage) and follows the same conventions: a Target hostname, output under _Processed\<host>\FortiGate-Log-Analyzer, the shared IOC.txt, runinfo.json provenance and a case window.

2  Requirements & setup

  • Windows with the built-in mshta.exe and Windows PowerShell 5.1 - both ship with Windows 10 / 11 and Server 2016+. Double-click FortiGate-Log-Analyzer.hta. No install, no admin rights, no third-party tools.
  • The parser is C# compiled at run time by PowerShell's Add-Type (the .NET Framework compiler that ships with Windows). If an application-control policy blocks run-time compilation, the run stops with ENGINE_FAIL could not compile the parser - see Troubleshooting.
  • If the .hta was downloaded, Windows may mark it as from the Internet: right-click → Properties → Unblock (or Unblock-File) before the first run.
  • Run it from a local folder (for example C:\Tools\FortiGate-Log-Analyzer). From a network share Windows zone policy blocks the UTF-8 file reader; the app falls back to ANSI file IO automatically, but local is best.
  • Sizing: about 15 seconds per GB of logs on a normal workstation; memory grows with the number of distinct addresses and sites, not with file size.

3  Getting the logs off the FortiGate

The app reads FortiOS key=value log lines (date=... time=... logid="..." type="..." subtype="..." ...) - the native format of every FortiGate. Any mix of log types can go in one folder; every file is sniffed and non-FortiGate files are listed and skipped.

SourceHowNotes
GUI downloadLog & Report → pick a log view (Forward Traffic, System Events, VPN Events, User Events, Antivirus, Web Filter, Application Control, IPS, SSL...) → set the time range → Download. One .log per view.The most common source in incident response. Downloads usually omit devname (the app reads the firewall's name from the System log instead) and each download stops at a row limit - busy views such as Forward Traffic may cover only hours. Overview flags the gap; export busy types day by day.
FortiAnalyzerLog View → select the device → download / export logs in raw (key=value) format, plain or .gz.Best coverage - FortiAnalyzer usually keeps weeks or months. Carries devname= on every line. CSV exports are not read in this version - choose raw.
SyslogThe FortiGate's syslog feed captured by any syslog server, in the default format (config log syslogd setting → set format default).A leading <189> priority or a syslog header before date= is ignored. CEF and CSV syslog formats are not read in this version.
Disk / memory logs via CLIexecute log filter ... then execute log display, captured to a text file.Works, but slow for large volumes and limited per call - prefer the GUI or FortiAnalyzer.
Collect broadly. Admin logins, configuration changes, HA and firmware events are all in the System event log; SSL-VPN and IPsec in VPN; captive-portal / LDAP / FSSO authentication in User; sessions in Forward Traffic (and Local Traffic for traffic to the firewall itself). The security-profile logs (Antivirus, IPS, Application Control, Web Filter, SSL, DNS) add the "what was caught" layer. Rotated and gzipped files, including concatenated multi-member .gz, are all read.

4  Quick start

  1. Folder… → pick the folder holding the exported logs (searched recursively), or File… for a single log. The line beside the buttons says how many FortiGate log files were found and how many other files will be skipped.
  2. Check Target hostname. It is filled from the logs when they name the firewall: devname=, or for GUI downloads the System log's "changed hostname global setting to ..." event (FortiOS writes it when the name is set and at every boot). If you type something different, an amber chip offers the logged name.
  3. Optional: IOC / keywords… - add terms before processing so every raw line is swept for them (see IOC sweeps).
  4. Process → analyze. The status line shows progress per file; the run loads automatically when the engine finishes.
  5. Start on Overview. Click any finding to open the table behind it.
Control panel after processing the synthetic FGT-ACME-01 folder: 8 FortiGate log files found (one README skipped), hostname read from devname=, output under _Processed\FGT-ACME-01\FortiGate-Log-Analyzer next to the app, run loaded with 20 findings.

5  Overview & findings

The Overview summarises the run (lines, files, log types, the time span the logs cover, the device name and timezone) and lists findings - one-line conclusions generated from every table by the app's rules, ranked CRITICAL → HIGH → MEDIUM → LOW → INFO. Each finding links to the table it came from. Below them, Log coverage draws the span of each log type against the overall window.

Findings on the synthetic week: an admin login from the Internet after 640 failures, IOC hits, a new admin account and VIP, an SSL-VPN login from an unusual country, an SMB sweep, a 3.3 GB upload, exposed RDP, malware that was allowed through, and AnyDesk allowed.
  • Input incomplete (CRITICAL) appears first whenever a file could not be read or was only partly decoded - every table is then missing those lines. Fix or re-export the files before relying on absence of evidence.
  • Coverage gap (MEDIUM) appears when one log type spans less than half the window of the others - nearly always a GUI download row limit. Conclusions from that log type only hold for its span.
  • Findings that count across a large table say when they were computed from the 6000-row preview; security-profile outcome totals (allowed / blocked / unknown) are always counted over every record. See How it works.
  • Copy the findings list (Help → link at the bottom) for case notes.

6  The tabs

Every tab is a set of tables with the same controls: a search box over all columns, severity (All rows / Flagged / High only), a UTC date window (an aggregate row passes when its First..Last span overlaps; an event row when its time falls inside), Export view → CSV (every row the view shows), Open full CSV (the complete table) and Copy for case notes, plus the forensic filters below. Shaded rows are flagged (red = high, amber = medium, blue edge = context); the Flags column says why. Click a row for every field. Columns are resizable. Hover anything - a button, tab, column header, flag tag or severity chip - for what it does or means.

Filters & pivoting

The second toolbar row holds the filters a firewall investigation keeps reaching for. Each appears only on tables it applies to, they combine, and clear all resets every one. Export view and Copy for case notes take exactly the rows on screen.

FilterWhat it doesTypical use
PivotOne indicator followed across every tab: an IP, a CIDR range (198.51.100.0/24), a user name or a host / domain, whole-token (1.2.3.4 does not match 11.2.3.45). Each tab and sub-tab button shows a ◆ count of matching rows, Overview lists every table it appears in, and the pivot stays on as you move. Click an IP in the row detail to pivot on it."Where else does this attacker IP / this account / this host show up?" - admin attempts, VPN, inbound sessions, UTM events and the timeline in one sweep.
Internet IPs onlyRows whose SrcIP / DstIP / RemoteIP / Src is a public address (by address class).Admin attempts and VPN logins from outside; UTM events involving external hosts.
Allowed / succeeded onlyWhat got through: accepted sessions, successful admin / VPN / user logins, tunnels that came up, security-profile events whose outcome was allowed.Separating noise (blocked scans, blocked malware) from what actually reached a host.
Off-hours onlyEvent rows before 07:00, from 19:00 or at the weekend on the firewall's own clock: each row is judged on the local date / time the firewall logged for it (the Local_Device column, with its tz= offset), so a run that crosses a daylight-saving change is right for every row. Rows without a logged local time are not guessed - they are left out and counted.Admin sessions, config changes and VPN logins at 03:00 local time.
CountryRows for one FortiGuard-geolocated country; the list shows the table's countries with their row counts.VPN logins and inbound sources from unexpected countries.
VolumeRows where a byte column reaches ≥ 10 MB, 100 MB or 1 GB.Bulk transfers - exfiltration and staging.
Pivot on 198.51.100.77: every tab button carries a ◆ count of matching rows (VPN 14, Traffic 2, IOC 27, Timeline 27), and VPN events shows the attacker's eight failed SSL-VPN logins, the tunnel coming up and the earlier IKE probes in one view.

Activity over time

Counts per hour (or per day for spans over ten days) from counters the engine keeps while it reads every line - the "when" behind the tables. One panel per question, at most four series each:

  • Admin logins - succeeded / failed / lockouts, with a method filter (HTTPS / GUI, SSH, console / other). A wall of failures is brute force; a success inside or right after it needs checking.
  • VPN logins (SSL-VPN up / failed, IPsec phase-1 errors) and user authentication (success / failure).
  • Traffic volume (bytes out to / in from the Internet; internal and inbound bytes one click away) and sessions (accepted / denied; inbound one click away).
  • Antivirus, IPS, web filter - malicious categories and risky applications, split by outcome (allowed / blocked / unknown).
  • Configuration changes (risky / other) and IOC hits from the raw-line sweep.

Toggle any series in its legend (the totals beside each name cover the range shown). Hover a bar for the exact counts; click it to set the date window to that day and open the table behind the chart. Choose hourly or daily bars and the clock - UTC or the firewall's own, judged per event. Every chart has a table view of its non-empty intervals.

Hatched intervals have no lines of that log type at all. An empty bar on a hatched background means the export does not cover that hour - no data, not no activity. On a GUI download whose Forward Traffic covers two hours of a week, the traffic panels are hatched everywhere else.

Activity over time on the synthetic week: the admin brute force is one tall burst of failures; SSL-VPN logins sit among IPsec scanning noise, with the attacker's failed logins in orange; two hours with no user-event lines are hatched.
These are pre-counted totals per interval. The pivot, search and other table filters do not narrow them - click through to the tables for that.

Admin access

Every admin login attempt (GUI / HTTPS / SSH / console) aggregated by source IP and by username, plus each successful login and logout in time order. TargetIPs are the firewall addresses the attempts hit - a WAN address there means admin access is exposed to the Internet. FailsIn24hBeforeOk is the largest number of failures that fell in the 24 hours before one of the successes.

Admin access by source: 198.51.100.23 failed 640 times, then succeeded (INTERNET-ADMIN-LOGIN, FAIL-THEN-SUCCESS, BRUTE-FORCE); the rest is Internet password spraying against the WAN address.
Successful admin logins and logouts. The attacker's session ends with state Config-Changed - the logout record itself says the session changed configuration.

Config & system

Config changes lists every configuration change the system log recorded: CfgPath (what kind of object), CfgObj (which one), CfgAttr (attributes, old→new), the admin and how they were connected. Notable system events keeps what is worth reading (alert / critical level, firmware, HA, backup / restore, admin-initiated actions) and leaves routine rotation and update noise in All event types.

The attacker's four changes from 198.51.100.23: a new super_admin account (ACCOUNT-CHANGE), a VIP and policy publishing RDP, and FortiAnalyzer logging switched off (LOGGING-OFF) - next to netops' routine address-object edits.
FortiGate persistence is usually one of: a new admin or API user, a VIP + policy opening a path in, an SSL-VPN user / group / portal change, an automation stitch, or logging turned down. All of these are flagged.

VPN

SSL-VPN logins per user and remote address with country, tunnel IPs and bytes; IPsec tunnels & peers per tunnel and peer (rows named (no tunnel matched) are IKE attempts from peers no tunnel is configured for - usually Internet scanning); and the VPN event stream. A successful SSL-VPN login from a country other than the one most logins come from gets UNUSUAL-COUNTRY.

SSL-VPN: jdoe logs in from the Netherlands after eight failures, while every other session comes from Australia.

User auth

Firewall user authentication (captive portal, LDAP, RADIUS, FSSO) by user and failures by source. One source failing for five or more different users is flagged PASSWORD-SPRAY.

Traffic

Direction comes from the interface roles in each session: wan is the Internet, lan / dmz are internal. The tables:

  • Internet destinations - outbound sessions per public destination: sessions, bytes out / in (per-interval deltas, so long sessions are not double-counted), sources, ports, services, applications.
  • Internal sources - per internal host: Internet upload / download, internal bytes, distinct destinations, users, MACs, device type.
  • Inbound from Internet - sessions arriving from WAN per source: denied (scanning) vs accepted.
  • Allowed inbound - internal destination:port pairs that accepted sessions from the Internet, with how they ended (Terminations): what is actually exposed.
  • Lateral (admin ports) - internal → internal sessions on SMB, RDP, WinRM, SSH, RPC, LDAP, Kerberos, SQL and VNC per source and port. 20+ targets = SWEEP.
  • Ports & services, Largest uploads (the 500 biggest single outbound sessions) and Actions.
Lateral (admin ports): 10.10.20.15 reaches 35 internal hosts on SMB inside four minutes (SWEEP). The normal pattern underneath - workstations talking to a handful of servers - stays unflagged.
Largest uploads: a single 3.3 GB session from 10.10.20.15 to 192.0.2.50 (app MEGA) - the exfiltration.
Allowed inbound: RDP on 10.10.20.15 reached from the Internet through the attacker's new VIP (ADMIN-SERVICE-EXPOSED).
Only traffic that crosses the firewall is logged: same-subnet traffic never appears, and a policy with logging disabled leaves no trace. Uploads to a forward proxy / SASE (Zscaler, Netskope and similar) are tagged SASE-PROXY and not scored - the proxy's own logs hold the per-site detail.

Security profiles

Every security-profile event's FortiOS action is mapped to an outcome - blocked, allowed or unknown - per record, and counted per table row, so a site blocked once and allowed once shows both and is flagged as allowed.

  • Antivirus - every detection with its outcome, file, signature, URL and checksum.
  • IPS - per signature, source, destination and port, with blocked / allowed / unknown counts.
  • Application control - per application and internal host. Remote.Access, Proxy and P2P categories are flagged; allowed higher than blocked.
  • Web filter by site (one row per site, source and category - a site that changes category gets a row for each) and Web filter categories - malicious, phishing, C2, proxy-avoidance, newly registered and similar categories are flagged.
  • SSL inspection and Other (DNS filter, anomaly / DoS, DLP).
Antivirus: an EICAR test file blocked, and a trojan (invoice_0915.pdf.exe) that the monitor-only profile let through - MALWARE-ALLOWED.
Application control: AnyDesk allowed on 10.10.20.15 (REMOTE.ACCESS-ALLOWED) and TeamViewer blocked on another host.

IOC hits, Timeline, Sources

  • IOC hits - the raw-line sweep by term and every matching line, plus Matches in tables: see IOC sweeps. Click a raw-line match and the row detail splits the log line into its fields, evidence first - virus, file name, URL, hostname, action, message - so nothing has to be read out of the raw string.
  • Timeline - admin sessions, config changes, VPN logins, antivirus / IPS / application first sightings and IOC hits merged on one stream, newest first.
  • Sources - every file found under the input with its status (read, read with N gzip members, PARTIAL, FAILED, skipped), the coverage of each log type, lines per day, and the device names the logs carry.
Timeline of the synthetic week, newest first: the IOC hits, the exfiltration window, AnyDesk, the VPN login, the configuration changes and the admin takeover in order.
Sources > Files: every candidate file and what happened to it. The README is listed as not FortiGate; the gzipped IPS log and the syslog-prefixed application-control log were read normally.

8  Worked example - one week at ACME

The screenshots in this manual come from a synthetic week of logs for a fictional company, ACME (firewall FGT-ACME-01, WAN address 203.0.113.10, all public addresses from the documentation ranges). Read in the order the findings suggest, the story falls out in a few clicks:

  1. Admin access - 198.51.100.23 fails 640 times over SSH and HTTPS, gets locked out four times, then logs in as admin over HTTPS. Its logout says Config-Changed.
  2. Config changes - in the ten minutes of that session: a new support_svc super_admin account, a VIP publishing 203.0.113.10:3389 to 10.10.20.15 with a policy allowing it, and FortiAnalyzer logging switched off.
  3. VPN - the next morning jdoe fails eight SSL-VPN logins from 198.51.100.77 (Netherlands) and then succeeds; every other user connects from Australia.
  4. Traffic > Allowed inbound - 198.51.100.77 uses the new RDP VIP to reach 10.10.20.15 repeatedly over two days.
  5. Security profiles - AnyDesk is allowed on 10.10.20.15; a trojan download to another workstation passes a monitor-only antivirus profile; phishing blocks on that workstation the night before.
  6. Traffic > Lateral - 10.10.20.15 touches SMB on 35 internal hosts in four minutes.
  7. Traffic > Largest uploads - 10.10.20.15 then sends 3.3 GB to 192.0.2.50 (MEGA) in one hour-long session.
  8. IOC hits - with 198.51.100.77 and mega.example in IOC.txt, every raw line mentioning them is listed with its full text.

Each step is one finding on Overview. The Timeline shows them in order.

9  IOC sweeps

There are two layers, and both appear on the IOC hits tab:

  • Raw-line sweep - terms in the IOC box (or the toolkit IOC.txt next to the app, merged at launch) when you click Process are searched in every raw log line. Matching is case-insensitive and whole-token: 1.2.3.4 does not match 11.2.3.45, evil.example matches sub.evil.example. Every hit keeps its full raw line, file and time.
  • Matches in tables - terms applied at any time, including after processing, immediately gather every result-table row that contains them.

When you Apply terms the loaded run was not swept for, the app offers to re-sweep: it re-processes the loaded run's own input, host and output folder (shown for confirmation) with the new terms - never whatever the control panel holds from another case.

IOC hits > Raw-line sweep by term: 198.51.100.77 in 26 lines (VPN, traffic, IPS) and mega.example in 12 web-filter lines.

10  Outputs & reloading a run

Each run writes to _Processed\<host>\FortiGate-Log-Analyzer\ next to the app (or the output directory you set):

FileWhat it is
<host>-FortiGate-<stamp>.jsonThe run the viewer loads: every table as a preview of up to 6000 rows with its true total, the full-data outcome statistics, the files read and the IOC terms swept.
<stamp>_<table>.csvEvery table in full. Event lists (admin sessions, config changes, notable system events, VPN events, antivirus, IOC hits, timeline) are written while the logs are read, in file order, so nothing is ever dropped from them.
runinfo.jsonToolkit provenance: app, version, host, input, files, case window and a triage summary per run (read by the Artifact Finder).
FortiGate-Engine.ps1The engine the app extracted for the run (overwritten each run).

Load existing run (.json)… reopens a run instantly without reprocessing. Runs written by earlier versions still load; they lack the full-data outcome totals, priority previews and input-completeness checks, so their outcomes are read from each row's action list (an allowed action anywhere on a row counts as allowed) and Overview says so. Re-process for exact results.

11  Command line & toolkit conventions

mshta "FortiGate-Log-Analyzer.hta" "<input>" ["<outDir>"] [/auto] [/from:yyyy-MM-dd] [/to:yyyy-MM-dd]
  • <input> - a log folder or file (processed straight away with /auto), a run .json (loaded), or an output folder (its newest run is loaded). Several inputs can be joined with |.
  • <outDir> - output folder; a _Processed\<host>\ path also sets the hostname.
  • /from: /to: - the case window (UTC, inclusive). It prefills the date filter and is recorded in runinfo; it only ever filters, never scores. Tick also limit processing to this window to make the engine skip lines outside it.
  • Target hostname is required before processing - it names the output folder, as in every toolkit app.

12  How it works

Engine

The .hta is the launcher and the viewer. On Process it writes its embedded PowerShell engine next to the output and runs it hidden; the engine's C# core streams every line of every file once, parses the key=value pairs, and aggregates. Times come from FortiOS eventtime (seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds since 1970, UTC); date + time + tz is the fallback. Everything shown is UTC; the device timezone is on Overview.

Previews and full data

The JSON holds at most 6000 rows per table so the viewer stays fast. The engine fills it with priority rows first - allowed or unknown-outcome malware, risky configuration changes, admin logins from public addresses, successful logins, accepted inbound sources, risky applications, malicious-category sites - then the most significant or newest of the rest. Antivirus, web-filter, application and IPS outcome totals in the findings are counted over every record. A table whose JSON is a preview shows an amber preview chip, and findings computed from a preview say so. Open full CSV always has every row.

Outcomes

Security-profile actions are mapped per record: blocked = blocked, block, deny, dropped, reset, clear_session, attachment-removed, quarantined, replaced; allowed = pass, passthrough, monitored, allow, accept, detected, exempt, log; anything else is unknown, reported as such and never assumed blocked.

Direction

Interface roles decide: wan = Internet, lan / dmz = internal. FortiOS gives IPsec tunnels, loopbacks and some zones the role undefined; on a VPN session (vpntype present, or an ssl. interface) that side counts as internal, so overlays using public or odd address space are classified correctly. For any other undefined role the address class decides, and Overview reports how many sessions needed that fallback.

Input completeness

Every file under the input is listed on Sources > Files, each with a label unique across all inputs (two selected folders that both hold an event.log show full paths), and IOC hits carry the full path of the file they came from. Gzip files are decoded by the app's own deflate decoder: each member's header (including optional extra / name / comment fields) is parsed and skipped, its compressed data is decoded to the real end of the stream, and its CRC and length are checked before the next member is read. Concatenated .gz files are therefore read completely, and nothing inside a header can be mistaken for log data; a CRC failure or an undecodable tail marks the file PARTIAL. Files that cannot be opened or break mid-read are FAILED. Either raises the CRITICAL Input incomplete finding.

13  Limits & judgment calls

  • The firewall only logs what crosses it and what its policies log. Absence of traffic in the logs is weak evidence; check the policy's logging setting and the coverage bars first.
  • GUI downloads are capped. A week of Forward Traffic from a busy site may cover hours. The Coverage gap finding tells you; export day by day or pull from FortiAnalyzer.
  • Fail-then-success is proven by timing, not identity: several admins behind one NAT address can trigger it. Check TopUsers and whether the successful account was one being guessed.
  • Public vs private on Admin access is by address class. Sites that use public space internally will see "Internet" flags for internal admins.
  • Thresholds (20 failures, 1 GB, 20 targets...) are starting points for triage, not verdicts. A backup server legitimately uploads gigabytes; a management server legitimately touches every host on SMB.
  • Not read in this version: FortiAnalyzer CSV exports, CEF-format syslog, FortiCloud JSON. Convert to key=value or export raw.

14  Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
ENGINE_FAIL could not compile the parser (Add-Type)Run-time C# compilation is blocked (AppLocker / WDAC / Constrained Language Mode, or EDR blocking csc.exe). Run the app on an analysis workstation where PowerShell is in Full Language mode.
No readable FortiGate key=value log files foundThe input holds no files whose first 8 KB contain logid= and type= - typically a CSV or CEF export. Re-export in raw / default format. Sources lists what was skipped.
CRITICAL Input incompleteSee Sources > Files for the error per file: a corrupt or truncated .gz, a file locked by another program, or no read permission. Re-copy or re-export it and process again.
Hostname not filled inThe logs carry no devname= and the System log has no hostname-setting event in its window. Type the firewall's name.
A table shows "preview: 6000 of N rows"Expected for big tables. Narrow with search, Flagged only or the date window, or use Open full CSV.
Instructions button cannot download the manualOffline, or GitHub unreachable. A previously downloaded copy opens instead; this manual is also in the repository's docs folder.
